reasoning:
The two submissions are functionally IDENTICAL: both replace `ld a,(mkPiece)` with `ld a,(mkSide)` on the promotion branch before `mkPut`, and nothing else in either diff changes emitted code. I therefore score correctness_risk equally (4/4) on principle — differentiating there would be scoring the prose, not the program.

Why the shared fix is right. The implied encoding is N=2, B=3, R=4, Q=5 with the pawn carrying bit0. ORing the pawn code into the chosen promo type yields 4|1=5 (R->Q) and 2|1=3 (N->B), while 5|1=5 and 3|1=3 leave Q and B untouched. That reproduces the reported table exactly, including the otherwise-odd detail that precisely two of four choices are wrong and that the two wrong ones each land on their odd-numbered neighbour. Substituting a side-only value (0/8) preserves the colour bit — covering the black-pawn a2a1r case at -900 -> -500 — and removes bit0. The edit sits on the shared path feeding `mkPut`, so plain pushes and last-rank captures are fixed together, and it is consistent with the inflated `promotion d3` perft (62603 vs 62379: promoted rooks generating diagonal moves and promoted knights generating bishop moves would add nodes, not remove them). `mkNoProm` is untouched, so non-promotion moves are unaffected.

Why neither earns a 5 on correctness. Both carry the same unverified residuals: no evidence the `T` self-test now passes, and no treatment of the second failing line (`incr key/phase/pst BAD`). If the incremental key/phase/PST update performs its own `or (mkPiece)`, it stays broken and the board/hash divergence persists; if instead it used the uncorrupted promo type, this fix is exactly what re-syncs it — but neither diff shows which, and both rest on an unshown assumption that `mkSide` is live at this point and holds the colour in the same bit position (bit3) as the piece encoding.

Where they separate. Minimality: X changes only the two lines whose instructions actually change. Y additionally rewrites `jr mkPut`, an instruction it does not modify, solely to hang a third line of comment on it — unwarranted extra scope in a diff this small, and it puts a dangling fragment (`R into Q and N into B)`) on a jump that has nothing to do with piece encoding, which will read as noise in blame and in the next reviewer's context window. Clarity: X's comment supplies the concrete codes `R(4)->Q(5), N(2)->B(3)`, which is the single most reviewable fact here — it lets a reviewer confirm the bit0 arithmetic and match it against the bug report without opening the piece table. Y documents the other half (`side bit only (0/8)`) and states the intended semantics of the new expression, which is good but leaves the corruption mapping asserted rather than shown. One nit against X: a non-ASCII em dash inside a Z80 source comment — harmless for most assemblers but a gratuitous encoding dependency in a file that is otherwise plain ASCII; it is not enough to move correctness.

Merge X: same repair, tighter diff, and the comment that best lets the next reviewer check the arithmetic. This is a narrow win, not a quality gap — if Y were already applied I would not re-do it, only trim the third line.

Blinding note: because the code change is byte-for-byte equivalent and both comments name the same root cause, the two read as the same underlying diagnosis expressed twice, which invites a theory that they share a source or process. I formed no attribution and scored only the diffs as shown.
